papers.title: Free energy landscape of Dense Associative Memory
papers.abstract: Using large deviations theory, we solve and obtain a general expression for the free energy functional for a broad class of associative memories, including dense associative memories. We illustrate the method by reproducing classical results for the Hopfield model. For a finite number of patterns, we derive the temperature-dependent free energy functional for dense associative memories featuring polynomial interactions and Log-Sum-Exponential (LSE) activation. We also obtain the disorder-averaged ground-state energy landscape of these systems in the extensive limit. Our analytical framework reveals how memory retrieval depends on the initial state in higher-order dense networks, and gives the exact error-free threshold for the LSE model. This method provides a systematic procedure for analyzing diverse, complex architectures in associative memory.

papers.title: Underdamped Stochastic Optimal Transport with Landauer boundary conditions: machine learning and analytical solution
papers.abstract: Finding optimal transport protocols for underdamped stochastic processes is a difficult yet important problem in control theory. In this paper we develop a direct method, based on machine learning, to find the optimal solution of the problem in the presence of non-linear boundary conditions, including those modelling the Landauer bit-erasure problem. The dynamics is steered from a single-peak to a double-peak distribution in position space, by only acting on a controllable external potential. The problem is highly non-linear, and analytical solutions are not available in general. We benchmark our numerical results with a perturbative expansion, which is expected to hold in a suitable overdamped limit.

papers.title: DNNs, Dataset Statistics, and Correlation Functions
papers.abstract: This paper argues that dataset structure is important in image recognition tasks (among other tasks). Specifically, we focus on the nature and genesis of correlational structure in the actual datasets upon which DNNs are trained. We argue that DNNs are implementing a widespread methodology in condensed matter physics and materials science that focuses on mesoscale correlation structures that live between fundamental atomic/molecular scales and continuum scales. Specifically, we argue that DNNs that are successful in image classification must be discovering high order correlation functions. It is well-known that DNNs successfully generalize in apparent contravention of standard statistical learning theory. We consider the implications of our discussion for this puzzle.

papers.title: Root-of-unity limit of the $A_{n-1}$ lens elliptic gamma function solution of the star-star relation
papers.abstract: We study the root-of-unity limit of the multi-component spin solution of the star-star relation whose Boltzmann weights are products of lens elliptic gamma functions, and whose spins take values in $\mathbb{R}^{n-1}\times(\mathbb{Z}_r)^{n-1}$. When one of the elliptic nomes tends to a primitive $2rN$-th root of unity, the quasi-classical expansion gives at leading order the classical star-star relation of the Bazhanov-Sergeev multi-spin model; at the next order, under the standard assumptions on the saddle points, a $(\mathbb{Z}_{rN})^{n-1}$-state solution of the star-star relation, which depends on $r$ and $N$ only through $rN$. Real $\mathbb{Z}_n$-symmetric configurations of the continuous spins give elliptic $\mathfrak{sl}(n)$ Kashiwara-Miwa type models labeled by $n$-torsion points. Extended to general primitive torsion points, these include the broken $\mathbb{Z}_{rN}$ model of Quano and Fujii, for which the star-star relation follows from their Yang-Baxter equation when $\gcd(n,rN)=1$. In the trigonometric limit the saddle point equations single out the spectral curve of the $\mathfrak{sl}(n)$ chiral Potts model of Bazhanov, Kashaev, Mangazeev and Stroganov, and the Boltzmann weights become those of that model.

papers.title: Faster-than-power-law decay of order parameter correlations in the two-dimensional RP$^2$ model: a rigorous result by vibe-proving
papers.abstract: We consider the RP$^2$ model on the two-dimensional square lattice with nearest-neighbor interactions. It is obtained by replacing the spin in the standard classical Heisenberg model with a director, which does not distinguish two opposite directions. Unlike the standard classical Heisenberg model or the O(3) nonlinear sigma model, the RP$^2$ (and its cousin RP$^3$) model allows point vortex defects classified by $\pi_1(RP^2)= Z_2$ in two dimensions. It is tempting to expect the $Z_2$ vortices to induce a phase transition analogous to the well-established Berezinskii-Kosterlitz-Thouless transition in the O(2) model (XY model) in two dimensions. Indeed, the possibilities of a critical phase or a critical point with power-law correlations of the order parameter in the RP$^2$ and RP$^3$ models have been discussed in the literature. However, the challenging nature of the problem has prevented a definitive conclusion on the phase diagram so far. In this paper, we report a rigorous mathematical proof by Artificial Intelligence (ChatGPT 6 Astra) that the absolute value of the two-point correlation function of order parameters at distance $r$ in the RP$^2$ and RP$^3$ models on the two-dimensional square lattice is bounded above by $C_\beta \exp{(-c_\beta[\log(2+r)]^2)}$ for any finite inverse temperature $\beta\ge0$, with positive constants $C_\beta$ and $c_\beta$ depending only on $\beta$. Namely, the correlation function decays faster than any power of $r$. The proof is formalized and verified in Lean; the formalization is publicly available at doi:10.5281/zenodo.23548847 . A heuristic argument based on a one-parameter effective theory ansatz at large distances combined with the rigorous correlation bound suggests (but does not prove) that the $Z_2$ vortices are always unbound at any nonzero temperature.

papers.title: Coordination three heals, coordination four is hard: the antiferromagnetic Potts model with a costly third state
papers.abstract: We study the ground states of the antiferromagnetic three-state Potts model in which the third state carries a single-ion energy cost $D_3$, on arbitrary lattices, and show that the difficulty of the ground-state problem is controlled by the maximum coordination $\Delta$ alone; on planar lattices with $\Delta\le5$ it is classified completely. On lattices with coordination at most three the third state heals frustrated bonds one for one: every graph of maximum degree three other than $K_4$ has an independent set of sites that meets every odd cycle and whose size equals the number $\operatorname{fr}$ of frustrated bonds of the Ising ground state. This identity also follows from known results on the chromatic vertex stability of graphs; we give a constructive proof. Hence $E_0 (D_3)=\min(D_3,1) \operatorname{fr}$ for all $D_3$, computable in polynomial time on planar lattices. In graph-theoretic terms, independent odd cycle transversal is solvable in polynomial time on planar subcubic graphs. On planar lattices with maximum coordination four, in contrast, deciding the ground-state energy is NP-complete for every fixed $0\le D_3<2$ and polynomial for $D_3\ge2$. The boundary is set by a local principle: a site of coordination $d$ in the third state relieves at most $\lfloor d/2\rfloor$ frustrated bonds, so the third state is useless once $D_3\ge\lfloor\Delta/2\rfloor$; this threshold is sharp for every $\Delta\ge3$ and reproduces the triangular-lattice point $D_3^*=3$ of the equivalent spin-1 Blume--Capel antiferromagnet. From a single Ising ground state the proof builds an exact ground state in polynomial time, which for quasicrystalline, foam-like and defective lattices with thousands of sites takes seconds to minutes.

papers.title: A Unified Framework for Locally Stable Phases
papers.abstract: We propose a unifying framework for characterizing pure and mixed state phases of matter across equilibrium, non equilibrium, and metastable regimes. We introduce the concept of locally stable states, defined by the operational property that any local operation (including post selection) can be reversed by a local channel. We prove that local stability is equivalent to a state being short range correlated, defined by the decay of both correlations and conditional mutual information. We demonstrate that these properties are invariant under locally reversible channels, thus defining locally stable phases. Furthermore, we prove that local stability implies both the decay of a family of nonlinear correlators, including the fidelity correlator, and the decay of correlations in the canonical purification, thus bridging the gap between mixed and pure states. Along the way, we establish two results which may be of independent interest: we show that post-selection on locally stable (short range correlated) states can be implemented via local channels and that quantum Markov chains can be characterized by the local computability of nonlinear observables.

papers.title: Fluctuation-dissipation structure of quantum geometry
papers.abstract: Geometry of quantum states is a fundamental research area with applications ranging from topological materials in condensed matter to variational algorithms in quantum information. Due to their relative simplicity, pure states are often studied, while mixed states are generally needed, e.g., to have nonzero temperature. Mixed-state geometry, however, is much more challenging and has so far lacked any structure relating distance and curvature, like the K\"ahler structure does for pure states. This work introduces that structure. We show that it has the physical meaning of fluctuation-dissipation---by identifying distance with fluctuations and curvature with linear response---and that it becomes the known structure for pure states, but is non-K\"ahler otherwise. This paints a simple picture that unifies fluctuation-dissipation and geometry of quantum states. It also applies on parameter spaces, as encountered in condensed matter or estimation theory. Our picture implies that the geometry contains all linear responses and fluctuations, proves the fluctuation-dissipation relation, explains that quantum geometry appears in any sum rule, and allows one to geometrically characterize generic transport behaviors. Closed and open systems are treated with equal ease.

papers.title: Kibble-Zurek dynamics beyond the thermodynamic limit
papers.abstract: The Kibble-Zurek mechanism (KZM) predicts the universal scaling of topological defect densities generated during continuous phase transitions, a result derived in the thermodynamic limit of homogeneous systems. Yet real materials are intrinsically finite and heterogeneous, raising the question of how nonequilibrium universality survives outside this idealized limit. Here we establish an ensemble-finite-size extension of the KZM that describes critical dynamics in collections of independent finite subsystems with distributed sizes. We test this framework using a polycrystalline model system undergoing a symmetry-breaking transition. We find that the density of topological vortices follows an apparent power law with an exponent approximately half that observed in single crystals. This reduced exponent emerges quantitatively from averaging over the experimentally measured grain-size distribution, without fitting to the measured vortex densities. Our results demonstrate that finite-size effects do not simply suppress KZ scaling but reorganize it into an emergent statistical scaling regime governed by system-size heterogeneity. This establishes microstructure and geometry as control parameters of nonequilibrium critical dynamics and provides a general strategy to engineer scaling behaviour in complex materials.

papers.title: Agentic Global Optimization of Site-Disordered Crystalline Materials
papers.abstract: Site-disordered crystals, in which several elements partially occupy the same atomic site, cannot be simulated atomistically without first resolving an explicit ordering, and the number of possible orderings grows combinatorially with supercell size. Because each candidate requires an expensive structural relaxation, locating the global-minimum ordering is a costly combinatorial search. Here, we present an agentic search in which a surrogate model, fitted to previously evaluated configurations, selects each subsequent candidate by balancing exploitation, uncertainty, and novelty. Four surrogates are implemented within a shared framework: an ExtraTrees ensemble, Bayesian ridge regression, sparse ARD regression, and an ALiEGNN-inspired graph ensemble. These are benchmarked against three traditional methods: random walk, Markov chain Monte Carlo, and a genetic algorithm across 14 test cases spanning 12 crystal structures, with exhaustively enumerated global minima as ground truth. The agentic surrogates reach the global minimum in 94% of runs, compared with 55% for the traditional methods, with a median 4.3-fold reduction in evaluations relative to the best traditional method. Bayesian ridge regression succeeds in all runs with the fewest evaluations. Applied to Na2/3FePO4, with coupled Na/vacancy configurational disorder and Fe2+/Fe3+ charge disorder, the framework recovers the experimentally reported ordering when charge states are encoded in the surrogate representation, demonstrating its extension to multi-sublattice disorder.

papers.title: Large deviations, gradient flows and fluctuating hydrodynamics for fractional diffusion
papers.abstract: This work is a step towards a general understanding of fluctuations for systems of particles described at large scale by fractional diffusion. First, we derive formally a Large Deviation Principle for the empirical measure of mean-field interacting particles with a L{\'e}vy-type noise. In the case of independent particles, this unveils a generalized gradient flow structure at large scales. Second, we derive and solve numerically a stochastic Partial Differential Equation describing the fluctuating hydrodynamics of this system. The results compare well with direct numerical integration of the particles' dynamics.

papers.title: Topological Quantum Error-Correcting Thresholds of a Symmetry-Enriched Toric Code
papers.abstract: We study the error thresholds of a new topological quantum error-correcting code under the independent bit-flip and phase-flip noisy channel. By mapping to classical spin-glass models, we find that if Pauli X and Z errors are equally probable, the threshold of vertex syndromes is improved by 30% compared to that of the toric code, while the threshold of plaquette syndromes is lowered. Both thresholds increase when the Z component is less likely than the X component, reaching 0.5 if the Z component is absent. An analytical proof justifies this special case of perfect correctability, and a disordered version of Peierls's argument establishes a lower bound for the vertex-syndrome threshold.

papers.title: Fock-space delocalization and its control in scarred-vs-ergodic dynamics
papers.abstract: Quantum many-body scarred dynamics in Rydberg-atom arrays is characterized by revivals, in which the system repeatedly returns to its initial state despite its many-body complexity. But how extensively does the wave function explore the space of allowed configurations between revivals? We address this question by quantifying the fraction of configurations occupied during PXP dynamics initialized from the paradigmatic polarized and N\'eel states, which respectively exhibit thermalizing and scarred dynamics. Despite their striking revivals, dynamics from the N\'eel state spreads over exponentially many configurations, yet occupies a vanishing fraction of the full space in the thermodynamic limit. Dynamics from the polarized state, by contrast, occupies a finite fraction of the configuration space, close to anticoncentration and random-state statistics, although chiral symmetry limits this fraction to one third. A weak quasiperiodic field enables the polarized state to occupy half of the configuration space by lifting the constraint imposed by chiral symmetry. The N\'eel state, however, requires a stronger field to reach a comparable anticoncentrated regime. As the field increases further, the occupied fraction decreases for both initial states, revealing a nonmonotonic dependence of Fock-space delocalization on field strength without necessarily implying localization.

papers.title: Quantifying Blinking Suppression and Probing Its Mechanism in PPD-Treated Single Quantum Dots
papers.abstract: Colloidal semiconductor quantum dots (QDs) are highly promising materials for various applications, yet photoluminescence intermittency (blinking) remains a key obstacle to their practical use. While recent advances have enabled partial or complete suppression of this effect, both the degree of suppression and the mechanism by which it occurs are often difficult to establish. In the present work we analyse the blinking suppression of single CdSe/ZnS QDs after treatment with p-phenylenediamine (PPD), recently discovered by Yang et al. We revisit the blinking mechanism in this system and show that it is governed predominantly by the trapping mechanism, rather than by Auger ionization as previously proposed. For data analysis we apply a threshold-free two-dimensional criterion recently proposed by Podshivaylov and Frantsuzov. The criterion is based on the relative quantum yield estimator $\langle \hat{Q} \rangle^{(s)}$ and the decay-rate fluctuation parameter $\hat{\xi}$. We found that PPD treatment significantly increases the relative quantum yield and leads to only a modest increase in $\hat{\xi}$, indicating that the dominant effect of PPD is to shift the distribution of the non-radiative recombination rate toward lower values, rather than to eliminate its fluctuations. We further suggest a number of possible mechanisms of PPD-induced suppression and propose critical experiments for their verification.

papers.title: Airy distribution of the quenched spectral form factor in non-interacting fermions
papers.abstract: For chaotic many-body systems as well as the random energy model, the logarithm of the (scaled) spectral form factor (SFF) exhibits two robust properties at late times: (i) self-averaging and (ii) a reflected-Gumbel distribution. Here, we demonstrate that both properties break down for $N$ non-interacting fermions on a lattice of size $L$ with an incommensurate single-particle spectrum. We show that the logarithm of the SFF, upon rescaling by $1/\sqrt{L}$, follows the Airy distribution, in stark contrast to the reflected-Gumbel law. Moreover, it is no longer self-averaging, as its mean and standard deviation are of the same order. While deviations from reflected-Gumbel statistics are generically expected for non-interacting systems, we find that an interacting integrable model exhibits reflected-Gumbel statistics at late times, mirroring the chaotic case and distinguishing it from non-interacting fermions.

papers.title: An internal mode shifts the depinning threshold of dissociated dislocations without changing universality
papers.abstract: Driven elastic manifolds exhibit a depinning transition whose large-scale behavior is governed by a nonequilibrium critical fixed point. Real interfaces, however, often possess internal degrees of freedom, raising the question of whether such modes alter depinning universality or only nonuniversal properties of the transition. We address this question for a dissociated dislocation, whose two Shockley partials define a fluctuating stacking-fault width driven by correlated random-alloy stresses. Comparing exact thresholds on identical disorder realizations with the width either free or frozen, we find that width fluctuations leave the depinning universality class unchanged: the roughness exponent $\zeta$ and correlation-length exponent $\nu$ remain the same even when the width becomes strongly fluctuating and locally multistable. The threshold, however, shifts. The shift is governed by the elastic crossover length of the internal mode rather than by multistability, and can have either sign. An infinite-range mean-field treatment misses this mechanism. With the physical two-partial elastic kernel and disorder calibrated against measured strengths, width fluctuations raise the athermal critical resolved shear stress by 10-35% over that of a rigid dissociated dislocation. An internal mode can thus be irrelevant at the depinning fixed point while remaining quantitatively important for where the transition occurs.

papers.title: Relaxation speed in quenched-random force fields
papers.abstract: Disorder is commonly expected to slow down relaxation, as in glasses and disordered magnets. Here we show that this need not be the case in general, by analysing the asymptotic relaxation rate of a Brownian particle in a harmonic background potential and a quenched-random Gaussian force field with conservative and non-conservative components. Combining weak-disorder perturbation theory, random-matrix theory, and numerical solutions of the Fokker-Planck equation, we show that the outcome depends on the geometry of the background and on the properties of the random forces. We identify two distinct mechanisms that shape the relaxation speed: an effective stiffening of the background by the disorder, as previously reported in one dimension, and interactions (repulsive and attractive) between the levels of the Fokker-Planck operator. Through level attraction, a common feature of non-Hermitian operators, non-conservative driving forces pull the slowest mode towards faster ones, which facilitates faster relaxation. In anisotropic backgrounds, both effects occur at second order in the disorder strength, enabling either slower or faster relaxation. In isotropic backgrounds, level interactions dominate and the disorder affects the degenerate slowest mode already at first order. The shift is then given by the left-most eigenvalue of a Gaussian random matrix and relaxation is generically slowed down. In backgrounds whose anisotropy is comparable to the disorder strength, level attraction is most effective by merging the slowest mode with its neighbour into an oscillating complex-conjugate pair. In this case, relaxation becomes faster on average once the random forces are sufficiently non-conservative. Our results draw a nuanced picture of how disorder affects the asymptotic relaxation speed in complex systems and uncover general mechanisms that are likely to apply beyond the current setting.

papers.title: Les Houches Lectures on Community Ecology: From Niche Theory to Statistical Mechanics
papers.abstract: Ecosystems are among the most interesting and well-studied examples of self-organized complex systems. Community ecology, the study of how species interact with each other and the environment, has a rich tradition. Over the last few years, there has been a growing theoretical and experimental interest in these problems from the physics and quantitative biology communities. Here, we give an overview of community ecology, highlighting the deep connections between ecology and statistical physics. We start by introducing the two classes of mathematical models that have served as the workhorses of community ecology: Consumer Resource Models (CRM) and the generalized Lotka-Volterra models (GLV). We place a special emphasis on graphical methods and general principles. We then review recent works showing a deep and surprising connection between ecological dynamics and constrained optimization. We then shift our focus by analyzing these same models in "high-dimensions" (i.e. in the limit where the number of species and resources in the ecosystem becomes large) and discuss how such complex ecosystems can be analyzed using methods from the statistical physics of disordered systems such as the cavity method and Random Matrix Theory.

papers.title: What do the fundamental constants of physics tell us about life?
papers.abstract: In the 1970s, the renowned physicist Victor Weisskopf famously developed a research program to qualitatively explain properties of matter in terms of the fundamental constants of physics. But there was one type of matter prominently missing from Weisskopf's analysis: life. Here, we develop Weisskopf-style arguments demonstrating how the fundamental constants of physics can be used to understand the properties of living systems. By combining biophysical arguments and dimensional analysis, we show that vital properties of chemical self-replicators, such as growth yield, minimum doubling time, and minimum power consumption in dormancy, can be quantitatively estimated using fundamental physical constants. The calculations highlight how the laws of physics constrain chemistry-based life on Earth, and if it exists, elsewhere in our universe.

papers.title: Mpemba effect as an entropy-production race:Finite-amplitude bounds on crossing times in Markovian relaxation
papers.abstract: Two canonical preparations evolving under a common final Markov generator can exhibit the Mpemba effect because they excite different relaxation modes. We bound the first crossing of their relative entropies by treating relaxation as an entropy-production race. The exact balance $-\dot D=\dot e_p$ implies that a meeting occurs when the accumulated \emph{difference} of normalized entropy-production rates, $\int_0^t(r_H-r_C)\,\mathrm ds$ with $r_\alpha=\dot e_p^{\alpha}/D_\alpha$, equals the initial logarithmic deficit $\ln[D_H(0)/D_C(0)]$. Global entropy-decay inequalities yield a lower crossing-time bound when the entropy-decay constant is bounded from below and the hot rate from above; we supply both certificates. A nonzero cubic moment of a slowest eigenfunction is sufficient for the modified logarithmic Sobolev constant to lie strictly below the spectral gap. Combining established relative-entropy comparison inequalities with Markov contraction and the actual mode amplitudes gives finite-amplitude crossing bounds without a small-deviation expansion. For an exactly strong, reversible three-state preparation these give $0.1659\le t_M\le0.1674$ in model time units, independently certified by outward-rounded interval arithmetic. This interval is narrower than $1\%$ and contains $t_M=0.1662209$. The conservative global-rate comparison used here gives only $t_M\ge0.042$. The hotter preparation starts $6.12$ times farther from equilibrium, yet it reaches $D=10^{-5}$ at $t=0.233$, compared with $t=0.844$ for the colder one. Mean energy crosses later than relative entropy. For a fixed driven generator, nonadiabatic entropy production governs the same balance. These results concern finite-state relaxation in a specified distance and do not predict water-freezing times.

papers.title: Guaranteed Slater Conditions for the Numerical Conformal Bootstrap: Fixing Instabilities in SDPB, Navigator Methods, and Skydiving
papers.abstract: The semidefinite programs (SDPs) of the numerical conformal bootstrap, and of S-matrix and quantum-mechanics bootstraps, are solved with primal-dual interior-point methods whose convergence guarantees rest on primal and dual Slater conditions: the existence of strictly feasible points on both sides of the duality. Many bootstrap SDPs violate these. The consequences range from slow convergence to inconclusive verdicts and the breakdown of the Skydive algorithm. We introduce "Slater tools", all acting within the PMP class accepted by SDPB. Diagnostics measure the Slater margins and, when a margin vanishes, extract the exposing certificate that identifies the degeneracy. Two independent cures follow. Transforms that provide rigorous bounds on the original SDP objective and that for the right parameter choices return the exact value. Facial reductions that use the exposing certificate to remove the degeneracies themselves. We reproduce, explain and resolve all known types of failures in a mixed-correlator 3d Ising setup. We show that the $X$-Slater condition (SDPB's primal) fails at every disallowed point in feasibility mode, holds in every navigator problem we tested, and can be guaranteed by one additional condition on the navigator function. We show that the folklore "instability remedy" of a twist gap works by removing degeneracies at the endpoints of the positivity conditions. These often stem from a mistake in factoring out the block prefactor but can also arise legitimately in channels that mix equal and unequal operator pairs. Finally we classify and remove all degeneracies of the published current-scalar bootstrap, among them one at $x=\infty$, thus incurable by any gap assumption, caused by unequal polynomial degrees within one matrix block.

papers.title: Theory of Convective Diffusion
papers.abstract: We obtain a hydrodynamic theory of diffusive-scale dynamics in one-dimensional systems with interacting sound modes in the absence of self-interactions. Chaotic systems generically feature three distinct Gaussian relaxation processes: besides normal diffusion, driven by microscopic noise stemming from fast-decaying non-hydrodynamic modes, collisions between sound modes lead to two additional channels: convective diffusion manifesting as an effective multiplicative temporal noise, and an effective additive noise generated by the surrounding hydrodynamic modes. Our theory also includes, as a subclass, integrable systems described by generalized hydrodynamics, representing a pure realization of convective diffusion. Focusing on convective diffusion, we obtain an exact closed-form expression for the higher-point dynamical correlation functions and contrast their structure with those of normal diffusion. Additionally, we show that in convective diffusion each sound mode features a universal non-Gaussian distribution of charge transfer in its comoving frame, thereby establishing anomalous fluctuations as a characteristic feature of diffusive-scale dynamics in integrable systems.

papers.title: Triplon thermal Hall response in a honeycomb-lattice $J_1$-$J_2$ Heisenberg antiferromagnet with Dzyaloshinskii--Moriya interactions
papers.abstract: We investigate triplon topology and the thermal Hall transport in a columnar valence-bond solid of a spin-$1/2$ honeycomb-lattice $J_1$-$J_2$ Heisenberg antiferromagnet. Inequivalent triangular sublattices, modeled by $J_2^A\neq J_2^B$, remove inversion symmetry at nearest-neighbor bond centers and allow in-plane Dzyaloshinskii--Moriya (DM) interactions. We identify the two symmetry-allowed in-plane DM vector patterns and present detailed results for the pattern parallel to the bonds including an out-of-plane magnetic field. Within a harmonic bond-operator treatment, we determine the triplon bands, their Berry curvatures and Chern numbers, and the triplon thermal Hall conductivity. The DM interaction and magnetic field generate nonzero Berry curvatures, but the numerically integrated Chern number of every isolated triplon band vanishes. Nevertheless, the energy-dependent Bose weighting of positive and negative Berry-curvature regions produces a finite thermal Hall response at nonzero low temperatures. We delimit the dilute-triplon regime in which the harmonic transport calculation is expected to be reliable. These results show that a vanishing Chern number band does not directly constrain the triplon response of a valence-bond solid. We also comment on the effects on the columnar valence-bond solid phase of a DM interaction between next-nearest-neighbor spins characterized by an out-of-plane vector pattern.

papers.title: Frustration-Induced $1/6$-Vortex-Paired Phase in a Kagome XY Model
papers.abstract: Geometric frustration can fractionalize vortices in two-dimensional XY systems, but a given frustrated model usually hosts only a single type of fractional vortex. Here we study a kagome XY model in which an antiferromagnetic coupling $J_1$ and a second-harmonic coupling $K$ favor two competing frustrated ground-state manifolds. For $K/J_1<1/9$, the ground states map onto those of the kagome three-state Potts antiferromagnet and support $1/3$ vortices; for $K/J_1>1/9$, they map onto those of the kagome Ising antiferromagnet and support $1/2$ vortices. At $K/J_1=1/9$, the two manifolds become degenerate, and bends in the domain walls between them carry $1/6$-vortex excitations. Tensor-network calculations show that a finite-temperature phase with quasi-long-range order only in $e^{6i\theta}$ emerges from this degenerate point, separating the $1/3$- and $1/2$-vortex-paired phases. This $1/6$-vortex-paired phase has no counterpart in either parent manifold, showing that competing frustrated manifolds provide a route to new fractional-vortex-paired phases.

papers.title: Only the immortal can (almost) flock while turning: Two-dimensional chiral immortal flocks, time crystals and non-universal sub-logarithmic roughness
papers.abstract: We study two-dimensional chiral ``dry'' (non-momentum conserving) ``immortal'' (number conserving) ``flocks'' (polar ordered active fluids). Noise driven fluctuations about the noise-free ``time crystal'' state, in which the velocity rotates uniformly in time, obey coupled Kardar-Parisi-Zhang-like equations for the local velocity orientation and a conserved concentration field; the latter field stabilizes order. Orientational fluctuations grow only sub-logarithmically, and number fluctuations are suppressed (``hyperuniform''); both exhibit nonuniversal scaling exponents. There are three different universality classes of disordering transitions.

papers.title: Finite-time Mpemba crossings with imperfect preparation
papers.abstract: Two preparations evolving under the same thermal Markov generator can reverse their ordering in relative entropy even when the hotter state retains a nonzero slow-mode component. We derive a sufficient finite-time crossing condition for arbitrary finite irreducible reversible systems. The condition compares the preparations' weights in the entire slowest eigenspace, including degeneracies, and gives an explicit upper bound using the separation from the next distinct decay rate. Exact finite-amplitude entropy comparisons also yield all-mode enclosures and bounds based on a retained spectrum with a controlled omitted tail. A preparation-error inequality converts finite-time sign margins into explicit probability tolerances; extensions account for temperature, generator, and stationary-reference uncertainty. We test the bounds on 2000 predefined network draws with four graph families and 4--64 states. There are 86 numerically located crossings, of which 45 satisfy the simple sufficient condition. In a selected eight-state example, retaining two nonstationary modes certifies a crossing before 1.55163, improving a certified slow-sector endpoint of 2.53951; the located crossing is near 1.26943. A reflecting diffusion in an asymmetric potential supplies a separate physical example, with systematic mesh refinement. Independent interval arithmetic certifies selected spectral bounds, finite-grid first crossings, and an entire preparation-temperature rectangle in a three-state benchmark. The theorem does not require exact slow-mode cancellation, while its numerical sharpness and detection coverage remain model dependent. These results concern relative-entropy relaxation and do not predict water-freezing times.

papers.title: Static and dynamic density correlations of interacting active Brownian particles
papers.abstract: We develop a stochastic Dean--Kawasaki field theory to predict the static structure factor and collective intermediate scattering function of interacting active Brownian particles. Starting from the microscopic overdamped dynamics, we derive coupled stochastic equations for the density and polarization fields using an angular-moment closure. Gaussian linearization then yields closed analytical expressions for static and dynamic density correlations in terms of propulsion speed, mean number density, interaction potential, translational and rotational diffusivities. The coupling between density and polarization predicts a crossover from exponential relaxation to damped oscillations despite the absence of inertia. For Gaussian-core potential, the predictions contain no fitting parameters. Brownian dynamics simulations show quantitative agreement at low activity and long wavelengths, and reproduce the crossover behaviour. For Weeks--Chandler--Andersen potential, the nonintegrable core makes both the Fourier transform of the potential and the self-interaction correction term in the Dean--Kawasaki field theory ill-defined. We therefore introduce an approximation that replaces the interaction potential with a passive direct-correlation function fitted separately at each density and temperature. This approximation requires no additional activity-dependent fitting parameters.

papers.title: Thermal conductivity of Lennard-Jones fluids from equilibrium thermodynamics
papers.abstract: We derive a general expression for the thermal conductivity of simple fluids within a thermodynamic transport theory (TTT) in which the Onsager coefficients of an interacting system are related to those of an ideal reference system through the ratio of the determinants of the Hessians of the relevant thermodynamic potential. The transported quantity is identified with an effective energy density proportional to the rms energy fluctuations of a small fluid cell. The result expresses the thermal conductivity as the product of its dilute-gas value and a function of equilibrium thermodynamic properties, namely the specific heats at constant density and at constant $\rho T$ and the temperature derivative of the latter, with no adjustable parameters. For hard spheres, it reduces to a previously verified expression in terms of the thermodynamic factor. The theory is tested against molecular dynamics results for the Lennard-Jones (LJ) and the truncated and shifted Lennard-Jones (LJTS) fluids in the supercritical region, for densities up to $\rho^*=0.8$, using equations of state based on perturbation theory. For the LJTS fluid, the mean absolute percentage error is below 8\% for all the temperatures considered. For the LJ fluid, the predictions are compared with those of the revised Enskog theory for Mie fluids, using the same equation of state: TTT gives smaller errors at almost all temperatures, with a significant improvement at low temperatures, where the errors are reduced approximately by a factor between two and three.

papers.title: Resolving the spinon hierarchy of the Heisenberg antiferromagnet
papers.abstract: A local spin fluctuation in the spin-$\tfrac12$ Heisenberg antiferromagnet creates an even number of fractional spinon excitations. We resolve its zero-temperature dynamical structure factor through six spinons directly in the thermodynamic limit. Beyond the established two-spinon contribution of $72.89\%$, the four-spinon response gives approximately $21.90\%$ of the integrated intensity and six spinons contribute a further $4.3\%$, bringing the response to about $99\%$ of both the intensity and first-frequency-moment sum rules. We derive momentum-independent first-moment fractions in the calculated sectors and a general upper-edge law $S_n\sim A_n(k)(\omega_{n,u}-\omega)^{(n^2-3)/2}$ for every even $n$ at nonzero momentum. The rapid growth of the edge exponent explains why the expanding multiparticle bandwidth carries very little high-energy weight, while higher sectors remain appreciable within the lower-sector continua.

papers.title: Lifting the mixed to the pure: quantum phases of matter from canonical purification
papers.abstract: Pure-state quantum phases are defined through finite-depth local unitary connections. This concept of phases has recently been generalized to mixed states in terms of locally reversible channels. In this work, we establish a fundamental relation between mixed-state phases and pure-state phases. We show that a locally reversible channel between mixed states can be lifted to a local isometry between their canonical purifications; thus, if two mixed states are in the same phase, then their canonical purifications are in the same pure-state phase. Furthermore, an explicit construction of the lifting isometry is given by ``half'' of the Petz recovery map, suggesting that the Petz recovery map \emph{without rotation} is enough to connect mixed state phases. We illustrate our results with two examples: toric code under bit flip noise and Chern insulator under fermion number noise.
